title: Dancing Swifties Shook the Ground—and Scientists Are Listening
summary:
In August 2023, 70,000 fans packed a stadium in Inglewood, California, for a Taylor Swift concert. As they danced, the ground beneath them began to tremble—so much that it created seismic waves, the same kind of vibrations produced by earthquakes. During one song, the energy released was comparable to a minor earthquake.

But this isn't just a fun fact. Human activity constantly generates seismic waves, and scientists are increasingly studying them. NFL games, for instance, have rattled stadiums enough to be detected by seismometers. Researchers even used the Seattle Seahawks' stadium to test earthquake sensors. Mining, traffic, and other industrial activities also produce their own ground vibrations.

On the flip side, events that halt human movement lead to 'seismic quiet.' During COVID-19 lockdowns, human-made seismic noise dropped by half in some areas. Similarly, during the total solar eclipse in April 2024, cities experienced a noticeable reduction in ground vibrations as people paused to watch the sky.

Why does this matter? Understanding human-made seismic waves has practical applications. Engineers can use this data to design buildings that better withstand both natural and human-induced shaking. City planners can analyze how crowds move during large events, improving safety and logistics. And for seismologists, filtering out human noise is crucial for getting a clear picture of natural earthquakes.

As one scientist noted, studying these vibrations helps us 'see' the Earth's movements more accurately. So the next time you're at a concert, jumping along to your favorite song, remember: you're not just having fun—you're contributing to real scientific data.
why_it_matters: Understanding human-made seismic waves shapes how stadiums, arenas, and transit systems are designed — the same places teenagers pack into every week — while also making instruments used to detect real earthquakes more accurate. This story shows how everyday public events can become valuable scientific data for engineering and disaster preparedness.

background_read: The Inglewood stadium in the article is SoFi Stadium (the Los Angeles-area venue that has hosted the Super Bowl and major concerts), and Taylor Swift's Eras Tour turned stadium shows into stadium-wide jumping experiments.

Crowd seismology became famous in 2011, when fans of the Seattle Seahawks — a professional American football team — celebrated Marshawn Lynch's playoff touchdown run so wildly that seismometers recorded the shaking; scientists nicknamed it the 'Beast Quake.'

Seismometers (instruments so sensitive they can detect ground movement smaller than a grain of sand and are normally used to monitor earthquakes) pick up all sorts of everyday shaking, from subway trains and trucks to ocean waves striking the coast.
During the COVID-19 lockdowns of 2020, those instruments measured a worldwide drop in human-made seismic noise, which some researchers called the 'great seismic quiet.'
The same effect appeared on a smaller scale during the April 2024 solar eclipse, when cities quieted as millions stopped moving to watch the sky.

perspectives.description: Crowd-induced shaking gives stadium managers and city officials hard data about how 70,000 people move and jump at once, which can improve crowd-control and evacuation planning. Monitoring these vibrations during giant events could help make concerts and football games measurably safer.

Human noise is also a kind of pollution for earthquake monitoring: in cities, small natural quakes can be hidden beneath the constant rumble of traffic, construction, and cheering crowds. If engineers and scientists confuse human shaking with natural signals, early-warning systems could be less reliable in urban areas.

What the Swift concert illustrates is that seismometers record all ground motion, whether natural or human-made. Global networks built to watch earthquakes have become an accidental archive of human activity — from lockdowns to eclipses to concerts — and scientists are learning to mine those records for insights about both Earth and society.

As low-cost sensors become smaller and cheaper, stadiums could be routinely instrumented to turn crowds into part of urban sensing infrastructure, feeding live data into safety and logistics systems. Better methods for filtering human noise would also let seismologists detect fainter natural earthquake signals earlier, strengthening future early-warning networks.
